blogs.title: xLSTM in Plain English: Can RNNs Make a Comeback?
blogs.description: A big-picture tour of why the authors revisited LSTMs in the Transformer era, what they changed, and what it means. We’ll unpack the two core ideas—exponential gating and new memory structures—and explain how xLSTM achieves linear-time, constant‑memory inference while matching or beating strong Transformer and State Space baselines in language modeling.

blogs.title: Exponential Gates: How xLSTM Learns to Change Its Mind
blogs.description: Gates decide what to remember or forget—but classic LSTMs struggle to revise earlier choices. This post demystifies xLSTM’s exponential gates, the normalizer that keeps signals well‑scaled, and the stability trick that prevents overflow. Using intuitive examples (like a running “best match” search), we show how xLSTM can overwrite memories when better evidence arrives.

blogs.title: From Numbers to Matrices: Inside xLSTM’s mLSTM Memory
blogs.description: Meet the matrix memory that turns an LSTM cell into a key‑value store. We explain how mLSTM writes with a simple covariance update (value × keyᵀ), retrieves with a query, and normalizes for stability—no attention matrix required. You’ll learn why this boosts capacity for rare or long‑range information and how removing hidden‑to‑hidden mixing makes it fully parallelizable.

blogs.title: Why Memory Mixing Matters: sLSTM and Real State Tracking
blogs.description: Some problems need true state tracking (think parity, matching brackets, or following entities in a story). This post explains sLSTM’s role: it keeps recurrent memory mixing and adds exponential gates, plus multi‑cell and multi‑head designs for richer interactions. We contrast this with models that avoid mixing (Transformers, many SSMs) and show where sLSTM shines.

blogs.title: Blocks, Not Just Cells: Building LLMs with xLSTM
blogs.description: How do you turn new cells into a full‑fledged LLM? We walk through xLSTM blocks, residual pre‑LayerNorm backbones, and why mLSTM uses pre up‑projection while sLSTM uses post up‑projection. We then summarize results: strong validation perplexity at 15B tokens, robust length extrapolation up to 16k, favorable scaling laws at 300B tokens, and high decoding throughput thanks to constant memory.

blogs.title: Where xLSTM Wins—and Its Trade‑offs
blogs.description: A practical guide to choosing xLSTM. We cover when linear compute and constant memory pay off (long contexts, high batch decoding, edge deployments), and the costs (matrix updates in mLSTM, sLSTM not parallel across time, careful forget‑gate init). We discuss mixing sLSTM and mLSTM blocks, expected contexts before memory saturation, and how to get started with the open‑source code.
